title: Human-large language model collaboration in clinical medicine: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Guoyong Wang, Kaijun Zhang, Jiyue Jiang, Chaonan Wang, Hui Bi, Haojun Liang, Zuoliang Qi, Ying Huang, Yu Li, Xiaonan Yang
verification: Abstract (structured results) read at PMC 2026-11-05: ten peer-reviewed studies to Jun 2025; diagnostic accuracy RR 1.59 (95% CI 0.08-32.74, non-significant, prediction interval crossing null); composite scores MD +4.88pp (CI +0.65 to +9.12) but prediction interval -31.65 to +41.42; no overall time difference (I2=70%); documentation improved while factual error rates stayed ~26-36%; H+AI did not consistently beat AI-only in three-arm settings. Authors' conclusion quoted: evidence 'preliminary yet highly uncertain and context-dependent'. Full text not read.
relevance: The honest summary the health topic needed: pooled evidence that human+AI beats neither AI-only nor human-only consistently, with a documented 'collaboration paradox' and error rates of 26-36% persisting alongside quality gains — and the authors' framing of clinicians as 'expert verifiers' paying a 'vigilance tax', which is exactly the verification-work pattern the catalogue's skills and oversight topics carry. This is the evidence-check on the more optimistic single RCTs already catalogued (Pakistan, China, Nigeria, Harvard).

title: Artificial Intelligence and Information Integrity: Latin American experiences (Policy Paper No. 34)

Subsequent replication debates make its 'matches twice its size' claim one to verify against independent reproductions before relying on it.

title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models

Its 4%→74% jump on one puzzle is often quoted without the scope: three narrow tasks, GPT-4-specific scaffolding.
